lelijine-stirnabude.features: Fruiting bodies bluish-violet, brownish-violet in colour
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized, rarely large. Cap 7-10 (15) cm across, flattened or even slightly depressed in the centre, fleshy, matt, violet, brownish-violet, bluish-violet. Gills the colour of the cap, adnate. Stem 5—9x1-3 cm, when young the colour of the cap, when old greyish-brown, violet-fibrous. Flesh whitish, violet, with a strong woody smell and taste. Characteristic features: mushrooms with a rather sharp, unpleasant woody smell, appearing in groups, sometimes in colonies. Grows in forests, parks, raised bogs, grassy places. Edible. Not liked by everyone because of its strong mealy, woody smell. Suitable for pickling.

lepse.habitat: In forests, parks or even gardens, only under birches
lepse.features: Flesh does not change colour, stem shaggy
desc: Fruiting bodies large. Cap 5—15 cm across, from yellowish-grey to greyish-brownish-black in colour. Tubes whitish, grey, greyish-brownish, 1-3 cm long. Pores whitish, grey, slowly turning brown when pressed. Stem 5-15x1-3.5 cm, thickening evenly towards the base, firm, shaggy with grey, brownish-black fibrils. Flesh white, grey, not changing colour when cut. Characteristic features: the colour of the cap and stem varies from grey to blackish. Grows in forests, parks, raised bogs and mires where birch is widespread. Very common. A popular edible mushroom.

lipnusis-tampriagrybis.habitat: Most often rotten coniferous wood, especially spruce
lipnusis-tampriagrybis.features: Yellowish-orange, slimy fruiting bodies, sparingly branched
desc: Fruiting bodies 3-6 (10) cm tall, sparingly branched, the tip of each branch with a few small teeth, tough, sticky, slimy, yellowish, yellowish-orange, like little flames among the mosses. Flesh tough, yellowish-orange, without a particular smell or taste. Characteristic features: very similar to the coral fungi, but their fruiting bodies are not slimy and their bases lack septa. Grows singly in forests, especially coniferous ones, most often on wood embedded in or hidden in the ground among mosses, and also on the ground. Edible, of low value. Very common, but not abundant.

margakote-guote.features: Cap, gills and stem yellowish, fruiting bodies slimy
desc: Fruiting bodies small, medium-sized. Cap 3-6 cm across, slimy, shiny, greyish-violet-brown, with a black tinge. Gills whitish, with a bluish tinge, adnate. Stem 3-10 (12)x0.5-1.5 cm in size, slimy, white, banded. Flesh white, not bitter, without a particular smell. Characteristic features: slimy fruiting bodies, the stem more than twice as long as the cap diameter. Spores large. Grows in coniferous forests among mosses and grasses, a dozen or more, one near another. Likes calcareous soil and the company of spruce. Very common, edible. Eaten fresh, together with other mushrooms.

maumedyninis-piengrybis.habitat: Larch stands, forests and parks with larch
maumedyninis-piengrybis.features: Cap yellowish-orange, barely zoned, gills turning greenish when pressed
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 3-8 (10) cm across, convex-flattened, depressed, surface with faint, narrow spots, yellowish-orange, the colour of an orange. Gills whitish-yellowish, later ochre-yellow, crowded, narrow, adnate, turning greenish when pressed. Stem 3-9x1-2 cm, the colour of the cap. Flesh whitish, firm, with a fruity smell, with white, bitter milk. Characteristic features: the white milk does not change colour once exuded; grows in forests and parks only under larches. Appears singly or in small groups. Edible. Uncommon.

Fruiting bodies medium-sized, large. Cap 5-10 (15) cm across, irregularly flattened, matt, greyish-brownish, brownish, fleshy. Gills crowded, broad, pale grey, adnate. Stem 3-8 (10)x1-3 cm, firm, fibrous, pale violet, bluish, greyish-bluish, firmly attached to the substrate. Flesh thick, white, whitish, with an unpleasant taste and smell. Characteristic features: a mushroom of open, grassy scrub and pastures; spores spiny. Grows in summer and autumn, singly or in groups. Edible, a valuable mushroom. Protected.

melsvakotis-nuosedis.features: Young gills violet, greyish-bluish, spores large
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 5-8 (10) cm across, convex-flattened, conical-bell-shaped, eventually flattened with a blunt umbo, very slimy, reddish-brown, chestnut-coloured. Veil white, bluish. Young gills bluish, violet, later greyish-brown, reddish-brown, adnate. Stem 7-12x0.5-2 cm, of uniform thickness, when young enveloped in a bluish, slimy veil which turns brown as the mushroom ages and cracks into irregular fragments. Flesh whitish, yellowish, odourless, not bitter. Characteristic features: slimy chestnut-coloured cap, stem bluish, violet. Grows in small groups in coniferous forests, especially sphagnum pine forests, less often in deciduous forests. Edible. Common.

melsvazale-umede.features: Cap greyish, greenish-bluish, streaked, gills and stem white
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized, rarely large. Cap up to 15 cm across, the cuticle peels well, slimy, shiny, violet, bluish, greenish-violet. Gills white, when old cream, adnate, subdecurrent. Stem 5-10 (12)x 1.5-3 cm, white, rarely with a violet tinge. Flesh white, not bitter, with a pleasant smell. Characteristic features: firm, massive fruiting bodies, cap with a bluish, violet tinge. More common in deciduous forests. Grows singly or in small groups, likes calcareous soil, most often in deciduous or mixed forests with oak and hazel. One of the most valuable brittlegills. Uncommon.

melsvejantysis-alskniabaravykis.habitat: Only under alders, damp, especially peaty places
melsvejantysis-alskniabaravykis.features: Young fruiting bodies straw-coloured, later yellowish-brownish
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized, sometimes large. Cap 5-10 cm, sometimes 12-15 (20) cm across, yellowish, yellowish-brown, reddish-brown, slimy. Stem up to 8 cm long, 1-2 cm thick. Characteristic features: flesh yellowish, in old mushrooms brownish, turning blue instantly when broken or cut, later turning brown. Grows in damp deciduous forests, forest edges, raised bogs, under alders, in lighter places, among grasses. Not rare, more common in northern Lithuania. Edible. Used fresh or dried, suitable for making mushroom flour.

melsvejantysis-piengrybis.habitat: Deciduous forests, especially oak, birch and aspen woods
melsvejantysis-piengrybis.features: Cap zoned, with a violet tinge, stem white, yellowish-brownish.
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap up to 10 cm across, concentrically zoned, slimy, from violet-brown to ochre-greyish-brown, not brittle. Gills whitish, later yellowish-brownish. Stem 3—7x1—3 cm, whitish-brownish. Characteristic features: flesh whitish, yellowish, mild in taste, with a pleasant smell; when broken or cut it stains bluish-violet, and the abundant white milk turns violet. Grows singly or in small groups, likes the company of oak, hazel, birch and aspen. Edible, but uncommon.

melsvejantysis-silbaravykis.features: Cap and stem white, cream-coloured, coarsely fibrous
desc: Fruiting bodies large, fleshy. Cap 8-10 cm across, but also grows much larger (up to 15 cm), matt, whitish, cream. Tubes and pores whitish, later yellowish. Stem 5—10x2—3 cm, white, when old hollow. Flesh white, turning blue quickly and very vividly when cut or broken. Characteristic features: cap, tubes, flesh and stem turn blue instantly at the slightest touch. Grows most often singly or a few fruiting bodies together, in dry coniferous and deciduous forests, likes the company of pine. Edible, not rare.

melsvoji-baltekle.features: Cap and stem with a bluish-violet tinge
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 3-5 cm across, flattened, depressed, matt, violet, brownish-blue-violet, the surface roughish. Gills white, cream, crowded, adnate. Stem 3-5x0.5-1 cm, fibrous, the colour of the cap. Flesh white, with a violet tinge, thin, with a mealy smell, not bitter. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies bluish, with a mealy smell, growing singly in deciduous forests; an indicator of calcareous soil. Grows in deciduous forests, likes the company of oak, linden and hornbeam. Rare, protected. Edible, of low value, but too delicate; it should not be touched.

melsvoji-stirnabude.habitat: Forest meadows, clearings, forest edges, parks, among grasses
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized, large. Cap 5-10 cm across, sometimes larger, even up to 15 cm, greyish-violet, greyish-bluish. Gills crowded, greyish-violet, adnate. Stem 5-8x 1-2.5 cm, greyish-violet, with white down at the base. Flesh whitish, thick, juicy, with a woody smell, not bitter. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies only faintly bluish (never vivid), likes open places. Grows singly or in small groups. Edible, rare. The Field Blewit is very similar to the Wood Blewit and Lepista glaucocana, but only its stem is bluish, while the cap is greyish-brownish, brownish-yellowish.

melsvoji-tauriabude.features: Strong aniseed smell, cap, gills and stem bluish-green
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 3-7 cm across, sometimes larger, matt, bluish-green, fading to greyish-greenish. Gills crowded, slightly decurrent, bluish-green. Stem 3-6x0.3-2 cm, the colour of the cap. Flesh greenish, bluish, thin, not bitter, with a strong smell of aniseed. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies bluish-green in colour. Grows in small groups, sometimes a dozen or more fruiting bodies together. Edible, but it might be more valuable in the perfume industry. One of the most fragrant agaric mushrooms. Common.

miskine-guote.habitat: Deciduous forests, parks, calcareous oak woods with linden and hornbeam
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 3-8 cm across, conical, later flattened, with an umbo, matt, relatively fleshy, yellowish-orange, brownish-yellow. Gills whitish, later yellowish, slightly decurrent, adnate. Stem up to 8 cm long and 1—1.3 cm thick, greyish. Flesh white, firm, without a particular smell or taste. Characteristic features: a mushroom of oak woods, the cap fleshy, quite similar to a chanterelle. Grows singly or 2-3 fruiting bodies together, dislikes shaded places. Edible. Uncommon.

miskinis-pievagrybis.features: Flesh turns red when cut or broken, aromatic
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 5-10 cm across, not fleshy, on a yellowish, ochre background covered with greyish-brown, brownish-pink scales. Young gills greyish-pink, later pinkish-brownish chocolate-coloured. Stem 5-10 (12)x0.5-1.5 cm, with a white ring, whitish-brownish, thickened at the base, without a volva. Characteristic features: the Scaly Wood Mushroom (A. langei) is very similar, but its fruiting bodies are larger and turn red more vividly. Grows singly or a few fruiting bodies together. Edible. Common. 19 species of this genus grow in Lithuania. All have pink, chocolate-coloured gills. Valuable edible mushrooms (the Yellow Stainer is mildly poisonous), with medicinal properties.

oranzine-musmire.habitat: Coniferous and deciduous forests, likes boggy places
oranzine-musmire.features: Cap vividly orange and stem softly orange, with zigzag fibrils
desc: Fruiting bodies large. Cap 5-12 cm across, bell-shaped, later flattened, with a blunt umbo, slimy, finely scaly in dry weather, very rarely with remnants of a white coating, ochre-orange, ochre, margins grooved. Gills white, broad, when old cream. Stem 8-12 (15)x1-2 cm, thickening towards the base, hollow, without a ring, yellowish-orange, finely scaly, with a volva that is white outside and yellow inside. Flesh white, soft, with a pleasant smell and taste. Characteristic features: cap helmet-shaped, prominently grooved. Grows singly, rarely in groups. Edible, but it can be confused with the Common Amanita (paprastoji musmirė), therefore collecting it is not recommended. Often grows together with the Tawny Grisette, but being orange in colour and finely scaly, especially the stem, it is easily distinguished.

oranzinis-leksciagrybis.habitat: Forest clearings, forest edges, roadsides, forest tracks, ditches
oranzinis-leksciagrybis.features: Orange fruiting bodies, without a stem, growing in groups
desc: Fruiting bodies 1-5 (10) cm across, shaped like a flat-bottomed saucer; old ones develop irregularly distorted margins; orange, orange-red, the underside paler, whitish, smooth or slightly granular. Flesh pale orange, thin, very brittle, without a particular smell or taste. Characteristic features: fairly large orange mushrooms, visible from afar. Grows most often in larger or smaller groups on sandy, humus-rich and even clayey soil, sometimes also among grasses. Edible, but more valuable as a beautiful, decorative mushroom. Common; medical scientists are interested in its properties.

palsasis-raudonvirsis.habitat: Boggy sphagnum birch woods, less often mixed forests
palsasis-raudonvirsis.features: Fruiting bodies white, greyish, small, flesh not changing colour when cut
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 3—7 cm across, when young hemispherical, later convex-flattened, greyish, most often with a yellowish-bluish or greenish tinge. Tubes white. Stem 7-10 (12)x1-2 (3) cm, the colour of the cap, fibrous, scaly. Flesh white, the colour does not change when cut. Characteristic features: the base of the stem turns green; grows in boggy places. Grows in boggy pine forests with birch and in fens. Edible, not rare. 16 species of the Leccinum genus have been recorded in Lithuania; all are edible, some of them rare, and therefore not important from a practical point of view. All Leccinum boletes and birch boletes are home and food for mycetophages. Jays, roe deer and other forest dwellers feast on these mushrooms.

palvasis-piengrybis.habitat: Deciduous and coniferous forests, birch woods
palvasis-piengrybis.features: Fruiting bodies more brownish, spores smaller than those of the Mild Milkcap
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 2-7 cm across, convex, flattened, depressed, matt, sometimes shiny, especially in dry weather, fibrous, reddish-brown, reddish-orange-brown. Gills cream, later ochre, thin, adnate; when broken or cut they exude white milk, which later turns yellow. Stem 3-6x0.5—0.9 cm, the colour of the cap or slightly paler. Flesh whitish, yellowish-brownish, with white milk that eventually turns yellow. Characteristic features: similar to the Mild Milkcap, only in this species the milk is white and turns yellow once exuded. Grows singly or in small groups. Common, edible, of low value.

Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 3-8 cm, but even up to 12 cm across, yellowish-brown, ochre-brown, greenish-brown, honey-coloured with blackish-brownish scales. Young gills whitish, cream, later brownish-brown; when young they are covered with a white, yellowish membrane. Stem 3-12x0.3-2 cm, yellow near the cap, yellowish-brown lower down, with a yellowish-brown, sometimes falling-off ring, dirty brown at the base. Flesh whitish, yellowish, thin, with a pleasant smell and taste. Characteristic features: cap with blackish-brownish scales, stem with a yellow, yellowish-brown ring. Grows on trunks of living and dead trees, snags, stumps, roots, most often in large groups. Edible, valuable, loved and collected by mushroom pickers.

paprastasis-piengrybis.habitat: Deciduous, coniferous and mixed forests, near spruce and birch
paprastasis-piengrybis.features: Cap spotted in places, stem swollen, hollow, brittle
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized, large. Cap 7-12 cm across, grows much larger, slimy, shiny, spotted, bluish-grey, violet-brown, fleshy. Gills white, later cream, broad, adnate, subdecurrent. Stem 5-12x1-3 cm, hollow, yellowish-brownish. Flesh up to 2 cm thick, bitter in taste, turning yellow when pressed or broken. The milk is white; once exuded it becomes greyish-greenish. Characteristic features: fairly robust fruiting bodies with a violet tinge. Grows in small groups. Edible, very common. As with the brown milkcap, it is advisable to soak it.

paprastasis-plempis.habitat: Deciduous and coniferous forests, parks, groves, scrub
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 3-5 cm across, rarely larger, thin-fleshed, smooth-surfaced, sometimes with the margins curled upwards, brownish-yellowish, brownish-yellow, fading. Gills yellowish, narrow, brownish, adnate. Stem 3—8x0.3—0.6 cm, the colour of the cap. Flesh thin, tough, yellowish, brownish, with a woody smell, not bitter. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies not fleshy, tough, not bitter, with a woody smell. Grows among grasses, most often in small groups, sometimes singly. Edible, very common.

paprastasis-trimitelis.habitat: Deciduous and mixed forests with oak, hornbeam, hazel
paprastasis-trimitelis.features: The cap can be distinguished from the stem only by the greyish-bluish hymenophore
desc: Fruiting body funnel-, trumpet- or horn-shaped, with a deep hollow reaching right down to the base of the stem, 5—12 cm tall, 3—8 (10) cm wide in the upper part. The inside of the fruiting body is dark brown, brownish-black, rough, scaly, elastic, the margins irregularly distorted. The hymenophore, on the outside of the fruiting body, is smooth or slightly folded, blackish-grey, ash-coloured, with a greyish-bluish bloom. Flesh pleasant in taste. Characteristic features: greyish-bluish-black fruiting bodies with a brown tinge. Sometimes grows in sizeable groups. Edible, not rare, praised in German literature.

Young fruiting bodies are the size of a hen's egg, whitish-greyish, sometimes only the upper part protrudes from under rotten leaves and twigs. The covering has 3 layers, the inner one of gelatinous consistency, so a mushroom pulled up feels softly squashy. All the life force is stored in the inner layer, which, when the covering bursts at the top, very quickly, sometimes within 2 hours, grows a stem 8-20 cm long and 1.3-4 cm thick, tapering at both ends. The receptacle is stem-shaped, honeycombed, spongy, white, with a bell-shaped, green, blackish-green, very slimy, stinking head. The stench can be smelled from a distance of 20—30 m; it attracts insects, and after they lick off the slime a white head with an opening at the top remains. Grows singly or in groups, fairly common. A vodka tincture of this mushroom was used to treat rheumatism. Medical scientists are still interested in it today. Young egg-shaped fruiting bodies are edible.

pavasarine-baltekle.habitat: Forest edges, parks, lake shores, riverbanks, scrubby pastures, among grasses
pavasarine-baltekle.features: A mushroom of open places, growing in spring
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 5-8 cm, rarely 10-12 cm across, white or softly yellowish, greyish-yellowish, convex, matt, fleshy. Gills whitish, cream. Stem 3-7 (10)x1-2 (3.5) cm in size, white. Flesh white, with a strong mealy smell. Characteristic features: grows in spring, singly or in small groups. Edible fresh, salted, dried. Common. Medical scientists are interested in its properties. One of the most valuable spring edible mushrooms. People in the Biržai, Pakruojis and Pasvalys areas call it greitgrybis ("quick mushroom"); it is quite popular.

pavasarine-tauriabude.habitat: Coniferous forests, most often old fire sites, burnt areas
pavasarine-tauriabude.features: Fruiting bodies reddish-brown, flesh with a strong mealy smell
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 3-6 cm across, flattened, irregularly depressed, funnel-shaped, finely fibrous, margins bent downwards, reddish-brown, brownish-orange. Gills cream, brownish, running far down the stem. Stem 3-6x0.3-1.3 cm, elastic, often bent, crooked, fibrous, the colour of the cap. Flesh whitish, when old brownish, tough, with a strong mealy smell, not bitter. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies tough, cap irregularly depressed, stem crooked, gills decurrent; appears only in spring. Grows singly or in small groups in pine forests, less often spruce forests, most often on bonfire sites. Edible; suitable for inoculating pine seedlings when planting burnt areas.

pelkine-umede.features: Cap red, shiny, gills white, when old yellow
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized, large. Cap 8-15 cm across, peels easily, damp, slimy, shiny when dry, red, purplish-red, the centre of a deeper colour. Gills white, cream, when old yellow, broad, adnate, free. Stem 5-12(15)x 1.5-3 cm, white, with pink streaks. Characteristic features: grows in bogs, flesh white, firm, not bitter. Appears singly or in groups in damp forests, especially sphagnum pine forests. Edible, very common. Similar to the Copper Brittlegill, but redder and not darkening.

pelkinis-kazlekas.habitat: Wet, boggy forests, most often among sphagnum, under young pines
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap grows up to 5-6 cm across, not fleshy, yellowish, greyish-yellowish, slimy. Tubes yellowish, pinkish-yellow. Stem 5—9x1-2 cm, usually bent, crooked, with a ring. Flesh yellowish, greenish, when old watery, thin, soft, not changing colour. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies not fleshy, growing in raised bogs among sphagnum. Appears singly or a few fruiting bodies together. Edible, but not equal to the Slippery Jack, the Velvet Bolete or the Jersey Cow Bolete. Of low value.

piengrybis-gruzdas.habitat: Deciduous and mixed forests, especially oak woods, shady places
piengrybis-gruzdas.features: Gills very crowded, narrow, white, flesh white, peppery-hot
desc: Fruiting bodies large, robust. Cap grows up to 20 cm across, matt, fleshy, firm, irregularly flattened, slightly depressed, white. Gills very crowded, narrow, white, cream, with a bluish sheen, adnate, subdecurrent. Stem 3-8x2-3 cm, firm, solid, white, cream. Characteristic features: white, large, firm fruiting bodies; the milk is white and turns bluish-greenish on reacting with air. Grows singly, more often in groups. Edible, uncommon in recent years. Protected.

piengrybis-jautakis.features: Fruiting bodies yellowish-brown, chestnut, fleshy, smooth-surfaced
desc: Fruiting bodies massive. Cap up to 15 cm across, fleshy, matt, dry, sometimes cracked, yellowish-brown, orange-brown. Gills cream, turning brown when pressed or cut, exuding abundant white milk, adnate. Stem 3-10 (13)x 1—3 cm, the colour of the cap. Flesh white, firm, not bitter, with an unpleasant smell, most often of herring, of fish. Characteristic features: the milk is milky white, gluey, sticky, very abundant, more abundant than in other milkcaps, turning greyish on drying. Grows singly, likes light, grassy, calcareous, clayey places. Edible; suitable for frying mushroom cutlets, which are no different from beef cutlets. Uncommon. Protected.

piengrybis-paazuolis.features: Cap zoned, greyish-yellowish-brown, grows only under oaks
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 3-8 (10) cm across, when young convex, later flattened, depressed, without an umbo, the surface fibrous, zoned, reddish or yellowish-brown, fading to a pale brownish colour. Gills whitish, cream, later orange-yellowish, yellowish-brownish, adnate. Stem 3-7x0.3-1.3 cm, brownish, darker in the lower part. Flesh brownish, thin, firm, not bitter, with white milk, slightly bitter in taste, turning yellowish after a few minutes on reacting with air. Characteristic features: the white milk turns yellowish once exuded. Grows singly or in small groups. Edible, common. After brief boiling in salted water the bitterness disappears.

piengrybis-paliepis.habitat: Coniferous (especially old pine forests), less often deciduous forests
piengrybis-paliepis.features: Gills yellowish, distant, milk white, turning yellowish once exuded
desc: The Fleecy Milkcap is very similar to the Peppery Milkcap, only its fruiting bodies are more robust, fleshier, with a cream tinge. Mushroom pickers probably do not distinguish these species and collect them as one - the Peppery Milkcap. In some localities, for example in Suvalkija, these mushrooms are quite popular. Valuable, edible. To reduce the bitterness they must be soaked for several hours in lightly salted water or boiled for 20—30 min, and the water poured away. Characteristic features: gills thicker, more distant, yellowish, and the milk is white and turns yellow on reacting with air, but does not turn greenish as in the Peppery Milkcap. Grows singly or in small groups in coniferous and mixed forests, rarely in deciduous ones.

piestinis-pirstunas.features: A very robust club fungus, fond of oak and beech communities
desc: Fruiting bodies large, club-shaped, up to 25 cm tall and 5 cm thick in the upper part, smooth or slightly wrinkled, ochre-yellowish, when old yellowish-brown, brownish-pink when broken or cut. Flesh soft, cottony, bitter when young. Characteristic features: robust yellowish-brown mushrooms shaped like a cudgel or club. Grows singly or in small groups, likes calcareous, humus-rich soil and shady places. In recent years very rarely found in our forests. The second-largest club fungus. Edible, but of low value. Must not be collected, because it is protected.

pilkalakste-tauriabude.features: Fruiting bodies ash-coloured, cap matt, its margins crimped
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 5-10 cm across, flattened, depressed, with an umbo, matt, fibrous, as if velvety, ash-coloured, yellowish-grey. Gills grey, brownish-grey, adnate or slightly decurrent. Stem 3-7 (9)x1—2 cm, of uniform thickness, dotted white near the gills, grey, brownish-grey. Flesh greyish, tough, not bitter. Characteristic features: cap slightly depressed, flesh with an unpleasant smell, spores slender. Grows singly or in small groups in coniferous, very rarely deciduous forests, likes calcareous soil. Edible, but of low value.

pilkasis-baltikas.habitat: Coniferous forests, especially pine forests, mixed forests
pilkasis-baltikas.features: Cap grey, brownish-grey, gills and stem whitish
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 3—5 cm across, when young conical, later convex-flattened, with an umbo, very fibrous, finely scaly, grey, brownish-grey, mouse-grey. Gills crowded, white, greyish, adnate. Stem 3-5x0.5-1 cm, of uniform thickness, white, grey, fibrous. Flesh thin, white, with a faint mealy smell, not bitter. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies smaller than those of the raibasis baltikas (Grey Knight), flesh white. Both species are very similar and hard to tell apart. Grows in groups. An edible, tasty mushroom. Very common.

pilkasis-kazlekas.features: Fruiting bodies dirty yellowish-grey in colour
desc: Cap medium-sized, rarely larger, 50-10 (12) cm across, greyish, dirty yellowish, greyish-brownish, slimy, the cuticle peels easily, margins often with remnants of the partial veil. Tubes greyish, greyish-brownish; pores white, grey, turning brownish when pressed. Stem 6—8x1—2 cm, the colour of the cap, thickening towards the base, with a white ring, older mushrooms with a grey ring. Flesh white, without a particular smell or taste, turning only faintly greenish-brownish when cut or broken. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies with a grey tinge, stem with a ring, grows only under larches. Appears in larch stands and in forests and parks with larch, in groups. Edible, uncommon.

pilkasis-piengrybis.habitat: Deciduous forests, especially grassy oak woods
pilkasis-piengrybis.features: Milk white, does not change colour, grows in light oak woods
desc: Fruiting bodies small, medium-sized. Cap 5-8 cm across, matt, fibrous, dry, velvety, dirty yellowish-brownish-grey. Gills greyish-cream, yellowish-brown. Stem 3—7x0.5-1.5 cm, white, later yellowish, the colour of the cap. Flesh white, turning red when broken or cut, with a pleasant smell, not bitter; the milk is white and does not change colour. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies greenish-brownish-grey, velvety. Grows in small groups, likes grassy oak woods. Found only in the Ginučiai oak wood, Ignalina district; it should be looked for in other forests too. Edible, but of low value.

Cap 3-5 cm across, shaped like a funnel with lobed margins, from grey, ash-coloured or greyish-brown to brownish-black. Underside folded, only in old caps slightly wrinkled, grey, cream, with a soft bluish tinge. Stem 4-7x0.5-0.8 cm, the colour of the cap. Flesh pale, tough, with a fruity smell. Characteristic features: cap lobed; in old caps the hymenophore is slightly wrinkled with a white bloom. Grows in groups in damp, grassy deciduous and mixed forests. Edible, of low value. Protected.

Fruiting bodies 3-8 cm tall, branching like a shrub: the branches and side branchlets dense, flat or round, with short, blunt, less often pointed, toothed tips, grey, brownish-grey in colour. Stem up to 3 cm tall and 6 mm thick, white or the colour of the branchlets. Flesh with a strong mushroomy smell. Characteristic features: tips of the branchlets blunt, rarely pointed or toothed. Grows singly or in small groups. Edible when young, of low value. Not rare, common in places.

pilkoji-tauriabude.habitat: Coniferous and mixed forests, scrub, among grasses
pilkoji-tauriabude.season: Summer (rarely), autumn (more often in the second half)
pilkoji-tauriabude.features: Fruiting bodies ash-coloured, fairly robust, with a sharp rotting, mealy smell
desc: Fruiting bodies large. Cap 7-12 (20) cm across, matt, fibrous, fleshy, ash-coloured. Gills whitish, later yellowish in colour. Stem 7-12x1-3 cm, whitish, greyish, brownish, firmly attached to the substrate. Flesh white, greyish, with a sharp, unpleasant woody, mealy smell, not bitter. Characteristic features: old caps are coated with a white bloom, as if floured. Grows in groups. Edible, praised by German mycologists. Common. Very similar to Alexander's Funnel, but differs in its ash-coloured fruiting bodies, unpleasant-smelling flesh and longer, firmer stem.

pilksvarude-stirnabude.habitat: Forest meadows, forest edges, parks, among grasses
pilksvarude-stirnabude.features: Cap, especially its margins, with watery spots
desc: Fruiting bodies large. Cap 5-12 (15) cm across, irregularly flattened, matt, with watery spots near the margins, which are sometimes upturned, brownish in colour. Gills crowded, thin, not broad, subdecurrent. Stem 3-6x1—2 cm, firm, the colour of the cap. Flesh yellowish-brownish, with a faint woody smell, not bitter. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies cream, brownish, with a faint woody smell, appearing in forest meadows and at forest edges. Grows singly or in groups in open, grassy places. Edible.

pilksvarudis-baltikas.features: Cap brownish, surface rough, stem white
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 3-7 cm across, when young conical, later flattened with an umbo, shaggy, finely scaly, greyish-brown, thin, fragile, sometimes with split margins. Gills broad, crowded, greyish, adnate. Stem 3-10x0.3-1.3 cm, white, fibrous, with a faint band of a ring-like remnant. Flesh thin, greyish, without a particular taste or taste. Characteristic features: grows in small groups or singly, fruiting bodies fragile. An edible, tasty mushroom. The Yellowing Knight (T. scalpturatum) is very similar, only it differs in its more fragile, more delicate and yellowing fruiting bodies.

pilksvazale-skydabude.habitat: Forests, parks, on dead deciduous trees, especially goat willows and aspens
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap convex-flattened, flattened, sometimes slightly depressed with a raised centre, matt, fibrous, grey, greyish-brown, with a greenish tinge, margins grooved. Gills white, quickly greyish-pink, pinkish-rose, crowded, narrow, free. Stem 3-7x0.2-0.8 cm, fragile, white, greyish, with a greenish tinge. Flesh white, thin, with a woody smell, not bitter. Characteristic features: most often found on fallen goat willows and aspens. Grows singly or in small groups. Edible, of low value. Not rare, quite common in places. 21 species of shield mushrooms (Pluteus) have been found in Lithuania; none are poisonous. Saprotrophs of wood and humus.

pilksvazale-umede.features: Cap greyish-green, green, fading, gills and stem white
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized, rarely large. Cap 5—8 (12) cm across, flattened, depressed or irregularly horizontal, the cuticle comes off easily and peels, dry, matt, greyish-green, yellowish-green, fading to greyish. Gills white, when old yellow, adnexed, adnate, slightly bitter in taste. Stem 3-8x1-2 cm, white, firm, brittle. Flesh white, firm, up to 1 cm thick, mild in taste, with a pleasant smell. Characteristic features: grows only under birches; one of the most common brittlegills. Grows singly or in small groups, under birches. A good edible mushroom. Very common.

pilksvazalis-piengrybis.habitat: Forests, parks, grows only under beeches
pilksvazalis-piengrybis.features: Young gills white, milk turning greenish
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 3-8 (12) cm across, when young hemispherical, later irregularly flattened, depressed, margins bent downwards, the surface slimy, shiny, sometimes spotted; when old it becomes matt, greyish-green, pale greyish-greenish-violet, greyish-brownish-greenish, spotted. Gills white, later cream, when old yellowish-ochre, slightly decurrent, with white milk. Stem 3-3 (6)x0.5—1.5 (2) cm, paler than the cap. Flesh whitish, turning grey when cut or broken, without a particular smell, bitter, with white milk. Characteristic features: greyish-greenish, not fleshy fruiting bodies. Grows in groups. Edible, very rare, protected.

pilksvoji-kreivabude.habitat: Forests, parks, on dead rowans, goat willows or aspens
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 3-10 cm across, fan-shaped, flattened, greyish, faded ochre, pinkish-yellowish, not fleshy. Gills white, greyish, yellowish, decurrent, not toothed. Stem lateral, 0.3-2.3x0.3-1 (1.5) cm. Flesh white, greyish, thin, with a mealy smell, not bitter. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies greyish, yellowish, brownish, growing several together on dead deciduous wood. Appears singly or in small groups. Common. A valuable edible mushroom.

pilvotaspore-zvynabudele.features: Spores large, fusiform, ventricose, cap brownish-ochre
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 4-6 (8) cm across, rarely larger, bell-shaped, flattened, with a smooth or cracked umbo, ochre, brownish-ochre, darker in the middle, fibrous, scaly, margins bent downwards, sometimes split. Gills white, broad, soft. Stem 4-10x0.4-1 cm, with a ragged ring, white above it, below it covered with scales and fibrils the colour of the cap. Flesh thin, white, soft, with a pleasant smell and taste. Characteristic features: this species is very similar to the Shield Dapperling (Lepiota clypeolaria), differing in its slightly larger, darker fruiting bodies and larger ventricose spores. Grows singly or in small groups, in much the same way as the Shield Dapperling. Edible, of low value. Uncommon.

pirstuotasis-auksliavarpis.habitat: Deciduous forests, parks, forest edges, scrub, wooded river slopes
pirstuotasis-auksliavarpis.features: Cap surface smooth or only slightly wrinkled
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 2—3 cm tall and 1—2 cm wide, bell-shaped, the top attached to the stem, from pale to dark brown, the margins paler, free; the surface longitudinally veined, grooved, wavy, wrinkled. Stem 5-10x1-1.5 cm, very brittle, yellowish, banded, pinkish, hollow. Flesh whitish, brittle. Characteristic features: cap fused to the stem only at the top, brown. Grows singly or in small groups. Edible. Rare.

placialape-kremble.features: Cap cracked, stem attached to the substrate by long strands
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized, sometimes large. Cap usually 5—10 cm, but grows even up to 15 cm across, fibrous, scaly, wrinkled, streaked, fissured, sometimes cracked, greyish-brown. Gills distant, broad, white. Stem 5-10x2 cm, white, at the base with long (up to a metre and more) white mycelial strands. Flesh white, thin, with a pleasant smell and taste. Characteristic features: broad, distant, thick white gills; cap radially streaked, margins sometimes split. Grows singly or a few fruiting bodies together on rotten branches, wood debris, in the ground. Edible, very common.

pukuote.features: Cap spotted, margins shaggy, milk white
desc: Fruiting bodies large. Cap 5—10 (12) cm, grows up to 20 cm across, flattened, depressed, shaggy in places, fibrous, margins rolled downwards, shaggy, yellowish-brownish, pinkish, fading to whitish. Young gills white, quickly becoming pink, when old creamy-brownish, adnate. Stem 3-8x0.5-2 cm, hollow, of uniform thickness, firm, brittle, brownish. Flesh white, later brownish, firm, brittle, crisp, without a particular smell, with a sharp, burning taste; the milk is white and does not change colour. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies yellowish-pink, growing only under birches. Appears in small groups and in groups. A common, good edible mushroom. Eaten salted or pickled. To remove the bitterness, as with other bitter-tasting milkcaps, it is advisable to boil it for 20 min, pour away the water and then prepare various dishes.

pusynine-rudmese-.habitat: Pine forests, especially young ones, forests with pine
desc: Fruiting bodies large. Cap 5-12 (17) cm across, fleshy, flattened, depressed, margins incurved, orange-red, with several concentric zones 1-3 mm wide, when old spotted green. Gills the colour of the cap; when broken or cut they exude orange milk that turns green after a while; adnate, subdecurrent. Stem 3-8x1-3 cm, the colour of the cap, spotted, turning green when pressed. Flesh juicy, white, yellowish, orange, firm; when broken or cut it exudes orange, greening, sharp-tasting milk. Characteristic features: yellowish-orange fruiting bodies turning green when broken or cut. Grows in autumn, even after frosts, less often in summer, in groups, at the grassy edges of pine forests. A very good edible mushroom, loved by everyone.

pusyninis-baravykas.features: Very similar to the Porcini, grows only under pines
desc: Fruiting bodies massive, large. Cap grows up to 25 cm across, pinkish, reddish-brown, purplish-brown, sometimes with a violet bloom. Tubes greyish, when old greenish. Stem 5-15 cm long, sometimes even 6-9 cm thick, yellowish-brownish, swollen in the middle. Flesh white, not changing colour when cut, with a pleasant smell and taste. Characteristic features: the cap and stem are more red, violet-purple in colour than those of the Porcini. Grows singly, often in groups, in pine forests. Very common. The most valuable edible mushroom. In great demand on the local and foreign markets. Medical scientists have become interested in these boletes.

raibasis-baltikas.features: Cap greyish-brownish, grey, shaggy, gills and stem grey
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 3-8 cm across, conical, later flattened, with a blunt umbo, coarsely fibrous, roughened, greyish-brown, grey. Gills grey, adnate. Stem 3—8x1-1.5 cm, of uniform thickness, fibrous, greyish, grey. Flesh thin, brittle, greyish, without a particular taste; old fruiting bodies have a woody, mealy smell. Characteristic features: likes the company of pine and open grassy places (roadsides, forest edges, clearings). Grows in groups in forests, especially coniferous ones, in pine forests. An edible, tasty mushroom, praised and loved by some mushroom pickers.

raiboji-umede.features: Cap purplish-brown, gills yellow, stem white
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized, rarely large. Cap 5-12 cm across, flattened, slightly depressed in the middle, reddish-brown, purplish or violet-brown, yellowish-bronze in colour. Gills white, when old ochre-yellow, adnate. Stem 5-9x1.5—3 cm, white, sometimes streaked with red. Flesh white, thick, brittle, mild in taste. Characteristic features: cap margins crimped, warty-grooved, the cuticle peels easily, stem massive. Grows singly or in small groups. Edible, of good taste. Uncommon, but widespread in the forests of Lithuania.

rasalinis-meslagrybis.habitat: Deciduous forests, parks, gardens, roadsides, squares
rasalinis-meslagrybis.features: Cap bell-shaped, stem with a ring near the base
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized, less often large. Cap up to 7 cm or even 10 cm across, bell-shaped, grey, brownish-grey, scaly, ridged, cracked. Gills black. Stem white, later grey, 7-10x1-2 cm. Flesh white, moreover with a pleasant smell and taste. Characteristic features: cap grey in colour, the margins as if frayed (crumbled). Grows several or a dozen or more fruiting bodies together in fertile soil, on rotted manure, on rotting deciduous wood. Edible when young, provided no alcoholic drinks are consumed. The active substance it contains, coprine, 1—2 hours after the meal, interacting with alcohol, causes changes in the blood; the heart rhythm and blood pressure are disturbed, nausea and vomiting occur, and a rash breaks out on the body. This substance has interested medical scientists for treating alcoholics.

raudongalvis-baltikenis.features: Cap and stem purplish-red, finely scaly
desc: Fruiting bodies large, fleshy. Cap 8-15 (25) cm across, brownish-red, brownish-yellow, violet-red, scaly. Gills yellow, adnate. Stem 5—15 (20)x 1—5 cm, yellow, covered with purplish-red scales, woody. Flesh firm, not bitter, yellow, thick. Characteristic features: fleshy, tough fruiting bodies, most often growing on pine and spruce, but often also on birch and oak stumps, especially near the ground (on roots). Appears singly or in small groups. Edible, more valuable than Prunes and Custard (Tricholomopsis decora), but so far not used as food, because it is tough and woody. Very common.

raudonkepuris-aksombaravykis.features: Cap brownish-red, stem without a network, red in the middle
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 3—8 cm across, matt, slightly velvety, bright red, brownish-red, faded brownish-brown. Tubes yellow, yellowish-greenish. Stem 3—8x1.3—2 cm, yellowish-orange near the cap, as red as the cap around the middle, yellowish-pinkish at the base. Flesh yellow, turning blue when cut, without a particular smell or taste. Characteristic features: underside of the cap yellow, greenish-yellow, flesh turning blue. Grows in deciduous and mixed forests, especially oak woods with hornbeam, linden, ash and hazel. Rare, edible. Protected.

raudonkote-umede.features: Cap shiny, gills white, flesh bitter in taste
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized, rarely large. Cap 5-10 cm across, convex, domed-hemispherical, later flattened, margins bent downwards, sticky, then dry, shiny, the cuticle comes off easily, red, cherry-coloured. Gills white, quickly becoming cream, ochre-cream, adnate. Stem 3-8x1-2 cm, white, with a red bloom or streaked with red, whitish at the top, the base tapered. Flesh white, firm, thick (up to 1.5 cm), bitter in taste. Characteristic features: the company of spruce, a red cap and a stem with a red bloom. Grows singly or in small groups. Common. Edible, but because of its bitter taste it should not be collected.

raudonvirsis.habitat: Deciduous, mixed, grassy forests, only under aspens
raudonvirsis.features: Stem shaggy with pale brown, later greyish- or blackish-brown scales
desc: Fruiting bodies large, fleshy. Cap grows up to 30 cm across, fibrous, orange-red, brownish-red, yellowish-red. Tubes whitish, grey; pores whitish, in old ones greenish, brownish-grey. Stem 3-20x3-6 cm, white, covered with greyish-brown, later blackish-brown scales and fibrils. Characteristic features: flesh white, quickly turning greyish-bluish, greyish-violet, greenish-brownish, blackish when cut or broken, with a pleasant smell and taste. Grows in deciduous, coniferous and mixed forests, only under aspens. Edible, very valuable.

rauksletasis-dyglutis.habitat: Coniferous and deciduous forests, especially spruce forests
rauksletasis-dyglutis.features: Fruiting bodies pale yellow, fading, spores round
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized and larger. Cap 5-10 (15) cm across, rarely larger, whitish, pale yellow, the surface smooth. On the underside whitish, yellowish, soft, brittle decurrent spines. Stem 3—8x0.5—2 cm, central or eccentric, white, yellowish. Flesh yellowish, when old slightly acrid. Characteristic features: cap slightly depressed, lobed and wavy, fleshy. Grows singly. Edible. The Terracotta Hedgehog (Hydnum rufescens Fr.) is similar, only its fruiting bodies are yellowish-orange, yellowish-brown in colour. Both species often grow next to each other; in earlier literature they were even considered identical. Edible. Common. Protected.

rauksletasis-gudukas.season: Summer, more often autumn (until the frost)
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 5-7 (12) cm across, bell- or helmet-shaped, eventually flattened, with an umbo; when young it is whitish with a greyish-violet bloom from the veil, when old yellowish, straw-coloured. Gills cream, yellowish-brown, adnexed. Stem 7-12 (15)x1-3 cm, of uniform thickness or slightly thickening downwards, ochre, yellowish, brownish, with a falling-off ring. Flesh whitish, yellowish, with a pleasant smell and taste. Characteristic features: mature fruiting bodies straw-coloured, stem with a membranous ring. Grows in groups, most often in pine and spruce forests. Very common. A good edible mushroom, loved by many mushroom pickers.

rauksletasis-trimiciukas.features: Hymenophore almost smooth, in old ones wrinkled
desc: Cap 4 (6) cm across, shaped like a deep funnel reaching even to the base of the stem, from grey to brown, fibrous, bluish-grey in colour, with a bloom. Hymenophore distinct, greyish-yellowish, from brownish to greyish-ochre in colour. Stem 2-5 (7)x0.3—0.8 cm, grey, greyish, yellowish-brown, the colour of the cap. Flesh grey, with a pleasant smell. Characteristic features: very similar to the Ashen Chanterelle, only the fruiting bodies of this one are larger, the hymenophore more distinct, with a bluish tinge. Grows in groups. Edible, of low value. Found rarely. Protected.

rausvarude-stirnabude.habitat: Coniferous and mixed forests, on needles, among grasses, in damp places
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized, rarely larger. Cap 3—8 cm, rarely 10 cm across, shaped like an irregularly depressed funnel (Clitocybe), reddish-brown, orange-brown, fading to yellow, yellowish. Gills whitish, yellowish, narrow, crowded, decurrent. Stem 2-5x1- 1.5 cm, usually eccentric, the colour of the cap, strongly attached to the substrate, so it is cut rather than pulled up. Flesh brownish, with an unpleasant woody smell, not bitter. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies resembling orange-brown funnels, caps depressed, grows in groups. Edible, of low value. Common.

rausvoji-musmire.habitat: Coniferous, less often deciduous forests, parks
rausvoji-musmire.features: Cap pinkish-brown, with grey warts, spores amyloid
desc: Fruiting bodies large. Cap grows up to 15 cm across, the fleshiest of all Amanitas, matt, dark or pale brown, ochre-pinkish-brown, concentrically covered with grey, greyish-brownish warts, as if scabby. Gills white, when old pinkish, spotted pinkish-brown. Stem 5-16x1-4 cm, greyish-brown, with a white ring, bulbously thickened at the base, without a volva or with only fragments of it. Flesh white, thick, soft, turning red when cut, without a particular smell. Characteristic features: stem without a volva, only with its ragged remnants. Cap and stem turn pinkish when broken. Grows singly or in small groups. Very common. The Germans write that it is a tasty mushroom.

rausvoji-slidabude.features: Cap and stem chestnut-coloured, spores tiny, round
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 4-6 cm across, reddish-brown, orange-brown, chestnut-coloured, slimy, the margins with ragged remnants of a white, brownish veil. Gills whitish, yellowish, free. Stem 5—9x1—2 cm, with a fibrous ring, above which it is whitish, smooth, below it shaggy, ragged, fibrous, slimy. Flesh thin, greyish, with a mealy smell, not bitter. Characteristic features: cap and stem very slimy. Grows singly or in small groups in deciduous, mixed and coniferous forests. Edible, of low value.

rievetasis-piengrybis.habitat: Deciduous forests with oak, hornbeam, aspen
rievetasis-piengrybis.features: Cap orange-brown, straw-coloured, zoned at the margins
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized and larger. Cap 3-10 cm across, domed, later convex-flattened, broadly depressed, the margins long remaining inrolled, bent downwards, slimy, pale ochre, straw- or orange-coloured, zoned, less so in the middle. Gills whitish, later brownish-yellow, forked, running down the stem. Stem 2-4x0.5-2 cm, white when young, later the colour of the cap. Flesh white, firm, turning yellow and brownish when broken or cut. The milk is white, does not change colour, slightly bitter in taste. Characteristic features: grows in oak woods or deciduous forests. Appears singly or in small groups in deciduous forests on calcareous soil with oak, likes its company. Rare. Edible.

ropliaodis-kukurdvelkis.habitat: Grassy forest clearings, forest edges, pastures, meadows, fallow land
ropliaodis-kukurdvelkis.features: Fruiting bodies shaped like a large blunt pear, surface cracked
desc: Fruiting bodies large, 7-15 cm tall and 5-12 cm across, bluntly pear-shaped, cylindrical-globular, when young white, when old brown; at first the surface is almost smooth, faintly spiny-warty, later it cracks, splits, becomes rough and eventually crumbles away, and, smoothed by the wind, becomes smooth. Young flesh white, spongy, when old turning brown; when the exoperidium cracks it crumbles and scatters, leaving only the lower, sterile, cup-shaped part of the fruiting body, which persists until the following summer and longer. Characteristic features: the surface of the fruiting body looks like crocodile skin. Grows singly or in groups. Edible when young. Common. Medical scientists are interested in its properties.

rozialakste-salmabude.habitat: Stumps, snags, windfalls of deciduous, less often coniferous trees
rozialakste-salmabude.features: One of the largest bonnets, spores amyloid
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 3-6 (8) cm across, slightly wrinkled, greyish-cream, greyish-brown, greyish, even whitish. Young gills white, greyish, when old softly pink. Stem 7-12x0.2-0.3 cm. Characteristic features: gills grey, when ageing greyish-pink; flesh thin, white, with a rather sharp radish smell, not bitter. Grows singly or in groups. Edible, of low value, very common. A strong wood saprotroph.

roziaspalve-geltonpede.habitat: Pine forests, especially their dry, ridged margins
roziaspalve-geltonpede.features: Cap and stem softly pink, gills grey
desc: Fruiting bodies smaller than those of the Slimy Spike and not slimy at all. Cap 3-5 cm across, dry, pinkish, with a rose tinge. Gills grey, greyish-brown, thick, distant. Stem up to 4 cm long and 1-1.5 cm thick, the colour of the cap, yellowish at the base. Flesh white, mild in taste. Characteristic features: grows in pine forests, especially older and sparser ones; fruiting bodies not slimy. Appears singly, less often a few fruiting bodies together. Edible, pleasant in taste, does not blacken when boiled. Uncommon.

rudakepuris-aksombaravykis.features: Cap chestnut-coloured, stem brown, of uniform thickness
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 5-8 (12) cm across, fleshy, reddish-brown or even blackish-brown in colour. Stem up to 12 cm long, 1-2.5 cm thick, without a network, firm, yellowish-brownish, paler near the tubes and at the base, of uniform thickness. Characteristic features: flesh white, with a pleasant smell and taste, turning blue when pressed or cut, eventually fading. Grows in smaller or larger groups, less often singly, in mossy coniferous forests. A tasty, valuable mushroom, loved by everyone. Fairly common. Used dried, fresh, pickled. This mushroom is often also called šilbaravykis (pine-heath bolete).

rudanugare-guote.features: Cap yellowish-brown with a chestnut-coloured disc in the middle
desc: Fruiting bodies small, medium-sized. Cap 3—5 (7) cm across, flattened, with an umbo, slimy, when dry shiny, thin-fleshed, brownish-yellowish, brownish-yellow, chestnut-coloured in the central part. Gills white, later yellowish, adnate. Stem 3—6x0.5—1 cm, whitish, yellowish, dotted white near the gills, with a faint, quickly vanishing ring-like remnant. Flesh thin, whitish, without a particular smell or taste. Characteristic features: a mushroom of hilly forests, the stem with a slimy remnant of the ring. Grows singly or in small groups in spruce forests with pine. Rare, edible.

rudasis-ausunis.habitat: Sandy coniferous and mixed forests, compartment lines, clearings, forest edges
rudasis-ausunis.features: Fruiting bodies dark brown, stem rudimentary or absent
desc: Fruiting bodies small, 2-8 cm across, when young round, later bowl-shaped, eventually shaped like an irregularly wavy saucer, the margins sharp, often split, pale brown, chestnut, dark brown in colour; the underside whitish-grey, brown, with a greenish tinge, granular, as if floured. Stem very short, rudimentary or entirely absent. Flesh brownish, brittle, with a pleasant smell. Characteristic features: most often grows on sandy soil. Grows singly, a few together, and sometimes even several dozen fruiting bodies together. Edible. Common.

rudasis-piengrybis.features: White milk bitter, does not change colour
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized, rarely large. Cap 3-8 (12) cm across, convex, later convex-flattened, the centre depressed, with a pointed umbo, margins bent downwards, dark reddish-brown, yellowish-brown, fading to greyish-brown. Young gills pale yellowish, later cream, reddish-brown, not narrow, adnate or semi-adnate. Stem 5—9 (10)x0.5—2 cm, paler than the cap. Flesh white, when old brownish, firm, brittle, with bitter white milk. Characteristic features: pinkish- or reddish-brown fruiting bodies, cap with an umbo. Grows in groups. Very common. Edible. To reduce the bitterness it should be soaked for 12-24 hours in cold salted water, then boiled for 20-30 min and the water poured away.

rudenine-kupstabude.habitat: Scrub, thickets, ditch sides, grassy roadsides, rarely forests
rudenine-kupstabude.features: Cap yellowish, brownish-brown, grows in open grassy places
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap grows up to 10 cm across, but sometimes reaches even 15 cm across, thin-fleshed, matt, greyish-violet, brown, yellowish-brown, irregularly flattened. Gills white, later pale cream. Stem the colour of the cap, 5-7 cm or even 9-12 cm long and 1-2 (3) cm thick. Flesh thin, tough, brownish, with a faint mealy smell, not bitter. Characteristic features: grows in large colonies of several dozen or even hundreds of fruiting bodies. Grows among grasses, in damp rich deciduous woods, raised bogs, sometimes along drainage ditches. Edible, of no special taste, common.

rudoji-voveraite.habitat: Deciduous, coniferous and mixed forests, damp, grassy places
rudoji-voveraite.features: Similar to the Winter Chanterelle, but in this one only the stem is yellow
desc: Fruiting bodies small, not fleshy. Cap 3-6 cm across, funnel-shaped, fibrous, matt, greyish-yellowish-brown, when dry greyish-yellowish. There are no gills, only unevenly branched, dirty yellowish, grey, yellowish-grey, vein-like wrinkles with a bluish tinge. Stem 4-6x0.3-1 cm, yellow, greyish-orange, orange-yellow, hollow, sometimes flattened. Flesh greyish-yellowish, with a mild, pleasant smell, not bitter. Characteristic features: underside of the cap yellowish-grey, with a bluish tinge. Grows in groups. Not rare.

sakotalakste-umede.features: Cap brownish-green, gills white, cream, crowded
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized, large. Cap 6-12 (14) cm across, the cuticle peels easily, matt, greyish-green, yellowish-green, green, with a grey or brownish tinge. Gills white, when old yellow, adnate. Stem 3—7x1—3 cm, white, darkening with age. Flesh white, not bitter, with a pleasant smell and taste. Characteristic features: gills forked near the stem, when old spotted pinkish; stem white, turning grey when old; grows more in coniferous forests. Grows singly or in small groups. Edible, a valuable brittlegill. Not rare.

sakotoji-skyletbude.habitat: Root collars of oak, hornbeam, linden, maple and other deciduous trees
desc: A many-capped, annual mushroom, very large, massive. Fruiting bodies grow up to 50 cm across. The fruiting body consists of a multitude, up to 100 and more, of branched, well-developed white stalks, each topped by a small umbrella-like cap 1-4 cm across, whitish, ochre, yellowish, pale or greyish-brown, fibrous. Tubes white, very short. Flesh firm, white, cream, with a pleasant smell and taste. Characteristic features: very similar to Hen of the Woods, differing in smaller caps, flesh that is not bitter and larger spores. The sclerotium from which this mushroom grows is perennial, so the Umbrella Polypore grows in the same place for many years. Found rarely, but more common than Hen of the Woods. Protected. Edible, tasty.

salnine-guote.features: Cap, gills and stem yellowish, fruiting bodies slimy
desc: Fruiting bodies small, medium-sized. Cap 3—5 cm across, rarely growing larger (6-10 cm), very slimy, when mature dry, yellowish-brown with a black tinge, when the slime has dried brownish-yellow. Young gills white, old ones yellow, spotted pinkish, decurrent. Stem up to 8 cm long and 1 cm thick, yellow, slimy. Flesh yellowish, with a pleasant smell and taste. Characteristic features: grows late in autumn, often after frosts. Mature fruiting bodies brownish-yellow. Grows one near another, but often in sizeable groups, in pine forests. Common. Edible. Very tasty fresh, worth the attention of mushroom pickers.

siauralakste-umede.features: Gills with a greenish sheen, spores smaller than those of the Milk-white Brittlegill
desc: Cap 8-12 cm across, its colour and shape as in the Milk-white Brittlegill (Russula delica) (white, yellowish). Gills white, crowded, narrow, subdecurrent, with a greenish shimmering tinge. Stem 3x2 cm, short, firm, white. Flesh white, firm, brittle, slightly bitter in taste. Characteristic features: very similar to the Milk-white Brittlegill, only the fruiting bodies are smaller; the species are very hard to distinguish morphologically. Grows singly or in small groups in deciduous and mixed forests, likes calcareous soil. Edible, valuable.

siaurinis-kelmutis.habitat: Forests, parks, gardens, roadsides, on deciduous and coniferous wood
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 3-8 cm across or larger, with a blunt umbo, irregularly flattened, fibrous and finely scaly in the central part, the margins smooth, grooved, from greyish-yellowish to brown. Young gills white, later cream, ochre-brownish, yellowish-brownish, adnate; when young covered with a membrane of the white veil. Stem 3-8 (10)x0.5-1.5 (2) cm, thickening towards the base, with a white ring, white, yellowish in the upper part, turning brown towards the base, with whitish fibrils. Flesh white, not thick, with a pleasant smell and taste. Characteristic features: cap more shaggy in the middle, stem white in the upper part, with a white ring. Similar to the Honey Fungus, which is currently divided into 3 species. Grows in forests and parks as a parasite and saprotroph, in large groups. Edible.

silinis-kazlekas.features: Stem without a ring, fruiting body not as slimy as that of the Slippery Jack
desc: The Weeping Bolete is very similar to the Slippery Jack, differing only in that its fruiting bodies lack the membrane, the stem has no ring, the cap is less slimy, and it appears in smaller groups. Grows in mature or old, grassy, less often young pine forests. A tasty edible mushroom. Common. Medical scientists are also interested in the properties of this mushroom.

silkavirse-sydabude.habitat: Deciduous trees: parks, squares, roadsides, less often forests
silkavirse-sydabude.features: Cap white and silky, shaggy, stem without a ring, with a large volva
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized, large. Cap 8-12 cm across, also grows considerably larger. At first bell-shaped, later convex, bluntly conical, eventually flattened, with an umbo, white, silky-shaggy, hairy, fibrous. Young gills white, old ones pinkish, free. Stem up to 12 cm and longer, without a ring, with a large, white, lobed volva. Flesh white, soft, with a woody smell and a pleasant taste. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies fibrous, growing only in hollows and injured places of deciduous trees. In anomalous cases the cap grows up to 23 cm across; one such was found in Druskininkai. Appears singly or a few fruiting bodies together. Edible, pleasant in taste.

silkiakvape-umede.habitat: Coniferous and mixed forests, especially pine forests
silkiakvape-umede.features: Cap colour very variable, often with a pink bloom
desc: Medium-sized. Cap 5-9 (13) cm across, the cuticle peels easily, sticky when damp, matt when dry, reddish-violet, reddish-bronze, with an ochre, greenish-yellow tinge. Young gills cream, later ochre, adnate, when mature free. Stem 3—8x1.5—3 cm, white, with a pink bloom. Characteristic features: flesh white, firm, not bitter, turning brownish or yellowish-bronze when pressed or broken, with a strong smell of herring (especially in old fruiting bodies and when rubbed between the fingers). Grows in summer and autumn, most often in sizeable small groups. Edible, common.

siurkscioji-zvynabude.habitat: Bosques de coníferas, sobre todo piceales húmedos y herbosos
siurkscioji-zvynabude.features: Al cortarla o romperla, la carne del sombrero y del pie se vuelve roja
desc: Muy parecida al parasol, se diferencia por sus carpóforos más pequeños, que suelen crecer solo en piceales húmedos; además, la carne de su sombrero y de su pie se vuelve de un rojo vivo al cortarla o romperla, lo que no es característico del parasol. Rasgos característicos: más pequeña que el parasol, carne que enrojece. Comestible, pero no tan sabrosa como el parasol; sin embargo, no hay por qué temerla, pues se reconoce fácilmente por su enrojecimiento y su hábitat, y en cuanto al sabor no es la peor de las setas. No es rara.

sketine-zvynabude.habitat: Bosques de coníferas y mixtos, lindes de bosque, bordes de caminos, lugares abiertos
sketine-zvynabude.features: Pie sin volva, una de las setas de láminas más grandes
desc: Una de las setas con sombrero más grandes; el sombrero alcanza 30 cm de diámetro y más; en los ejemplares jóvenes la superficie es lisa, pronto se vuelve áspera y agrietada, después pardo-escamosa. Láminas blancas, después crema, de hasta 3 cm de ancho. Pie 10-33x1-4 cm, con pequeñas escamas pardo-grisáceas y un gran anillo blanco, engrosado en bulbo en la base, sin la volva característica de las amanitas. Carne blanca, esponjosa, de olor y sabor agradables. Rasgos característicos: carpóforos grandes, carnosos, escamosos, que crecen solo en bosques de coníferas, con más frecuencia en pinares. Aparece aislada o en pequeños grupos. Se recolecta con gusto. Especialmente sabrosa frita en mantequilla. No se recolecta junto a las carreteras, porque es posible una intoxicación por los contaminantes acumulados en ella.

skiauteretasis-zagaris.habitat: Bosques de coníferas y de frondosas, parques
skiauteretasis-zagaris.features: Carpóforos blancos, grisáceos, puntas de las ramas ensanchadas
desc: Carpóforos ramificados, de 2-6 cm de altura, que crecen aislados o en grupos, blancos, amarillentos o incluso con un matiz pardo. Ramas varias veces bifurcadas o dicotómicas, con las puntas agudas, marcadamente dentadas. Pie de hasta 2 cm de largo, a veces totalmente ausente. Carne blanca, sin olor ni sabor particulares. Rasgos característicos: puntas de las ramas profundamente dentadas. Crece aislada o en pequeños grupos sobre el suelo de los bosques; una seta de aspecto atractivo. Comestible, de escaso valor. Poco común.

skroblinis-raudonvirsis.habitat: Bosques de frondosas, bajo carpes, avellanos, robles
skroblinis-raudonvirsis.features: Carpóforos más pequeños que los de otros boletos del género Leccinum, sombrero pardo grisáceo
desc: Carpóforos pequeños. Sombrero de 5-10 cm, raramente 15 cm de diámetro, mate, arrugado, a veces agrietado, pardo grisáceo sucio, pardo negruzco verdoso. Tubos grisáceos, poros blanquecinos. Pie 5-15x1—3 cm, blanco, cubierto de fibrillas pardo-blanquecinas, manchado de azul o de verde en la base. Carne blanca, que al corte se vuelve pardo-negruzca violácea. Rasgos característicos: pie blanco, con fibrillas pardas. Crece en bosques de frondosas y mixtos con carpe, aislado o en pequeños grupos. Prefiere suelos fértiles y calizos. Comestible, poco común. Protegido.

skujine-musmire.features: Carpóforos erizados de verrugas a modo de escamas
desc: Carpóforos grandes. Sombrero de 8-12 (20) cm de diámetro, de joven hemisférico, de viejo aplanado, a veces ligeramente deprimido, cubierto de verrugas escamosas y puntiagudas, carnoso, macizo. Láminas blancas, después crema, muy apretadas, libres, con numerosas laminillas. Pie 10-15 (20)x2-4 cm, que se engrosa hacia abajo pero se estrecha en la misma base, con un anillo fibroso, áspero, erizado. Carne blanca, gruesa, de olor y sabor agradables. Rasgos característicos: esporas amiloides, anchamente elípticas. Crece en verano, raramente en otoño, aislada, en bosques de frondosas. Termófila. Calcícola. Muy rara. Comestible, pero no se recomienda recolectarla, porque se encuentra muy raramente; debería incluirse entre las especies dignas de protección.

skydine-zvynabudele.habitat: Bosques de coníferas y mixtos, parques
skydine-zvynabudele.features: Esporas anchamente fusiformes, grandes, margen del sombrero y pie fibrosos
desc: Carpóforos medianos, pequeños. Sombrero de 3-5 (8) cm de diámetro, campanulado, con un mamelón pardo liso, y en toda la superficie finamente escamoso pardo-amarillento sobre fondo amarillento. Láminas blancas. Pie 6-12x0,5-1 cm, del color del sombrero, con un pequeño anillo flojo, deshilachado, pronto caedizo, por debajo del cual está erizado de fibrillas o escamas blancas, amarillentas. Rasgos característicos: carpóforos fibrosos, escamosos, pie con anillo. Carne blanca, blanda, de olor y sabor agradables. Crece aislada, raramente en pequeños grupos. Comestible, pero de escaso valor. Común. No se recomienda recolectarla.

smiltyninis-silbaravykis.habitat: Bosques arenosos de coníferas y de frondosas
desc: Carpóforos medianos, raramente grandes, carnosos. Sombrero de 5-10 cm de diámetro, mate, pardo rojizo, de color castaño, pardo amarillento. Tubos y poros blancos, después amarillentos. Pie 5—8x1—3 cm, sin retículo, casi del color del sombrero. Carne blanca, firme, de olor y sabor agradables, inmutable al corte. Rasgos característicos: carpóforos firmes, de color castaño. Crece aislado o de 2-3 carpóforos juntos en bosques de frondosas, de coníferas y mixtos, le gusta la compañía del roble. En Lituania es más común en los pinares arenosos, en los lugares más luminosos. Comestible, excelente, pero poco común.

sokoladine-dirvabude.habitat: Bosques, parques, matorrales, turberas altas, riberas de ríos
desc: Sombrero de 5-8 cm de diámetro, convexo-aplanado, con mamelón, mate en la madurez, margen estriado, pardo violáceo grisáceo, chocolate, que palidece a pardo grisáceo. Láminas pardo claro, pardo tabaco, con un matiz violáceo, estrechas, apretadas, con la arista como incrustada de blanco, subdecurrentes. Pie 5-9x0,5-1,5 cm, con un anillo membranoso blanco; por encima del anillo el pie está punteado de blanco y estriado, por debajo es del color del sombrero. Carne blanca. Rasgos característicos: láminas estrechas, apretadas, pie con anillo marcado, pleurocistidios en forma de bolo (lageniformes-fusiformes), grandes. Crece en lugares húmedos y herbosos, en grupos. Comestible, pero de escaso valor. Muy rara, fácil de reconocer; debería incluirse entre las especies dignas de protección.

stambioji-slidabude.habitat: Bosques de frondosas y mixtos húmedos y herbosos, turberas altas, matorrales
stambioji-slidabude.features: Sombrero y pie de superficie lisa, pie sin volva
desc: Carpóforos grandes. Sombrero de 5—12 cm de diámetro, aplanado, con mamelón, viscoso, sedoso con tiempo seco, crema, color carne. Láminas parduzcas, apretadas, libres. Pie 7—13x1—3 cm, blanco, con anillo blanco, sin volva. Carne blanca, blanda, con olor a harina, no amarga. Rasgos característicos: esporas pequeñas, no amiloides. Crece de unos pocos carpóforos juntos, en grupos, en bosques de frondosas y de coníferas herbosos y húmedos. Poco común. Comestible, de escaso valor. Muy parecida es la limacela viscosa (L. illinita), pero sus carpóforos son más pequeños y muy viscosos.

stambioji-tauriabude.habitat: Bosques de frondosas y mixtos, lugares calizos y herbosos
stambioji-tauriabude.features: El mayor de los clitocibes, carpóforos pardo-amarillentos, pie largo
desc: Carpóforos muy grandes. Sombrero de 10-30 cm de diámetro, ampliamente deprimido, de joven mate, de viejo brillante, parduzco, amarillo parduzco. Láminas crema grisáceo, largamente decurrentes. Pie 8-15x2-4 cm, del color del sombrero. Rasgos característicos: carpóforos muy grandes, carne no amarga, aromática, con un leve olor a almendra. Crece en grupos en lugares soleados y herbosos de bosques de frondosas y mixtos y de parques, formando «corros de brujas». Comestible. Poco común.

stambusis-nuosedis.habitat: Bosques herbosos, mixtos y de frondosas
stambusis-nuosedis.features: Sombrero pardo amarillento, débilmente fibroso, esporas grandes
desc: Carpóforos grandes. El sombrero alcanza 12-15 cm de diámetro y más, de un bonito amarillo, pardo amarillento, amarillo leonado, viscoso con tiempo húmedo, mate con tiempo seco, carnoso. Láminas jóvenes blanquecinas, crema, con un matiz violáceo, de viejas pardo amarillentas, adnatas. Pie 8-13x1-2 cm, blanquecino junto a las láminas, más abajo amarillo, amarillo ocre, con bandas en zigzag amarillo ocre fibrosas, pilosas y erizadas. Carne blanca, gruesa, no amarga, con olor a levadura.
Rasgos característicos: carpóforos grandes, amarillos, el pie claramente erizado en bandas anulares; aparece solo bajo abedules.
Crece con mayor frecuencia de unos pocos carpóforos juntos, en bosques de frondosas. Comestible. No es raro.

sultingasis-piengrybis.features: Látex blanco, abundante, que tras un tiempo más largo se vuelve grisáceo y verdoso
desc: Setas de tamaño mediano. Sombrero de 6-8 cm de diámetro, carnoso, bellamente abombado, margen curvado hacia abajo, ondulado (en los viejos), fibroso, leonado amarillo parduzco, naranja parduzco, sin matiz rojo. Láminas crema, crema amarillentas, subdecurrentes, estrechas (de hasta 2 mm de ancho); al romperlas fluye abundante látex blanco. Pie 5-6x1-2 cm, firme, junto a las láminas en la base estrechado, del color del sombrero. Carne crema, amarillenta, no amarga, de olor poco intenso, con abundante látex blanco. Rasgos característicos: muy parecido al lactario volemo (L. volemus), se diferencia por sus carpóforos más pequeños sin matiz rojo. Crece en pequeños grupos bajo tilos, robles y arces, entre hierbas. Termófilo. Comestible, muy raro; debería incluirse en el Libro Rojo de Lituania.

svelnioji-kelmabude.habitat: Tocones, tocones altos, árboles derribados de pino o de pícea
svelnioji-kelmabude.features: Crece casi solo sobre madera muerta de coníferas
desc: Carpóforos pequeños. El sombrero alcanza 7 cm de diámetro, superficie lisa, pardo amarillenta, pardo anaranjada, amarillo parduzca. Láminas jóvenes crema grisáceo, pronto gris violáceo o gris azulado, finalmente pardo negruzco verdoso. Pie 3-10x0,3-1,5 cm, amarillento junto al sombrero, pardo amarillento más abajo, sin anillo. Carne amarillenta, de olor y sabor agradables. Rasgos característicos: muy parecido al hifoloma rojo ladrillo (geltonraudė), solo que los carpóforos son más pequeños, el sombrero pardo amarillento, no fibroso. Crece en grupitos más o menos grandes. Comestible, muy común. De escaso valor. Se diferencia de las armilarias por sus láminas pardo negruzcas verdosas, la superficie lisa del sombrero y el pie sin anillo.

svelnusis-piengrybis.habitat: Bosques de coníferas, sobre todo piceales, también bosques mixtos
svelnusis-piengrybis.features: Carpóforos más pequeños que los del lactario volemo
desc: Carpóforos pequeños. Sombrero de 3-7 cm de diámetro, en la madurez aplanado, con o sin pequeño mamelón, superficie lisa, viscosa, brillante, mate con tiempo seco, amarillo anaranjado, naranja parduzco. Láminas jóvenes crema, después del color del sombrero, estrechas, apretadas, finas, adnatas; el látex es blanco. Pie 3-7x0,3-1 cm, del color del sombrero, frágil. Carne blanquecina, después naranja pálido, firme, no amarga, con olor a avellana; el látex es blanco. Rasgos característicos: carpóforos anaranjados, naranja amarillentos; el látex blanco no cambia de color al contacto con el aire. Crece aislado o en pequeños grupos. Común. Comestible.

sviesiakraste-guote.features: Carpóforos naranja parduzcos, pie esbelto, que se estrecha hacia la base
desc: Carpóforos pequeños. Sombrero de 3-5 (7) cm de diámetro, de joven campanulado, después aplanado, raramente algo deprimido, naranja parduzco, amarillo parduzco en el centro, el margen más pálido. Láminas blanquecinas, parduzcas, decurrentes. Pie 5-10 (12)x0,5-1 cm, parduzco, estrechado en la base. Carne delgada, parduzca, sin olor ni sabor particulares. Rasgos característicos: el pie suele ser el doble de largo que el ancho del sombrero; el sombrero es parduzco en el centro. Crece aislado en bosques de frondosas, en lugares húmedos y herbosos. Comestible. Raro.

sviestine-plempe.habitat: Bosques de coníferas y de frondosas
sviestine-plempe.features: Sombrero y pie pardos, de color castaño, láminas blancas
desc: Carpóforos medianos y mayores. Sombrero de 3—7 (9) cm de diámetro, superficie lisa, viscosa, seca en los viejos, pardo rojiza, de color castaño. Láminas blancas, apretadas, adnatas. Pie 3-8 (12)x0,5-2 cm, correoso, del color del sombrero. Carne blanca, de olor y sabor agradables. Rasgos característicos: pie que se engrosa claramente hacia la base, con vello blanco. Crece en grupos, le gustan los lugares musgosos. Comestible, apreciada. Muy común. Una forma muy parecida de la colibia mantecosa es la variedad grisácea (C. butyracea var. asema), solo que sus carpóforos son más pequeños, de color gris, gris parduzco. Comestible, apreciada. Muy común.

tamprusis-kazlekas.features: Carpóforos correosos, que no temen las heladas, crecen en grupos
desc: Setas de tamaño mediano. El sombrero alcanza 8 cm, con menos frecuencia 12 cm de diámetro, amarillo muy oscuro, pardo amarillento. Tubos de hasta 1 cm de largo, amarillo grisáceos, de viejos pardo verdosos. Pie 2-10x 1-2 cm, del color del sombrero, correoso; a menudo varios carpóforos están soldados por la base. Carne pardo amarillenta, de vieja con matiz rosado, muy correosa, de sabor suave. Rasgos característicos: carpóforos muy correosos, a menudo crecen varios en un mismo lugar; en Dzūkija también se le llama nakcižieda («la que florece de noche»), porque supuestamente los carpóforos brillan de noche. Crece sobre todo en pinares secos y arenosos, en grandes grupos. Una seta sabrosa; los carpóforos viejos son muy correosos y no deberían consumirse.

taureline-juosvabude.habitat: Entre hierbas, bosques, parques, riberas de ríos, orillas de lagos
taureline-juosvabude.features: Sombrero y pie de color pardo negruzco
desc: Carpóforos de tipo clitocibe (Clitocybe), de tamaño mediano. Sombrero de hasta 8 cm de diámetro, en forma de copa, profundamente deprimido, brillante, negruzco, pardo negruzco. Láminas pardo grisáceas, apretadas, largamente decurrentes. Pie de 5-10 cm de largo y hasta 1 cm de grosor, del color del sombrero. Carne delgada, correosa, pardo grisácea, de sabor suave. Rasgos característicos: láminas decurrentes, esporas grandes, anchamente elípticas, amiloides. Crece de varios o más carpóforos juntos, entre hierbas. Comestible, pero de escaso valor. Rara.

tikrasis-juodbaravykis.features: Superficie del sombrero aterciopelada, en los ejemplares viejos agrietada y resquebrajada
desc: Carpóforos macizos, carnosos, de aspecto sombrío. El sombrero alcanza 12-15 cm de diámetro, mate, aterciopelado, pardo grisáceo negruzco sucio, pardo oliva; de viejo agrietado, con la carne de las grietas verdosa; el margen verdea al presionarlo. Tubos parduzcos sucios; poros de los ejemplares jóvenes grisáceos, después pardo verdosos, finalmente pardo negruzcos. Pie de 5-10 (12) cm de largo y hasta 3,5 cm de grosor, del color del sombrero, fibroso. Rasgos característicos: carne grisácea, que al romperla o cortarla se vuelve rojiza, después adquiere un matiz verde azulado o incluso negro, de olor y sabor bastante desagradables. Crece aislado, raro. Protegido.

tikrasis-zvynbaravykis.habitat: Bosques de frondosas: robledales, abedulares y bosques de álamo temblón
tikrasis-zvynbaravykis.features: Escamoso, erizado, la carne al corte se vuelve rojiza y ennegrece
desc: Carpóforos grandes. Sombrero de 5-15 cm de diámetro, cubierto de grandes escamas grises, pardo grisáceas o incluso negras, carnoso. Tubos blanco grisáceos, de viejos parduzcos, de hasta 3 cm de largo, que se vuelven rosados al presionarlos. Pie 8-15x1—3 cm, de grosor uniforme, gris, de viejo pardo negruzco o incluso negro, firme, con un anillo o solo su resto, fibroso-erizado. Carne grisácea, que al cortarla o romperla se vuelve rosada, después palidece a gris negruzca. Rasgos característicos: sombrero escamoso, pie erizado con anillo. Algunas fuentes indican que no es comestible. Muy raro; hasta ahora encontrado solo en los bosques del Parque Nacional de Žemaitija. Reliquia de los bosques primarios de Lituania. Termófilo. Protegido.

tikroji-umede.habitat: Bosques de coníferas, de frondosas y mixtos
tikroji-umede.features: Sombrero mate, pardo rosado, con matiz violáceo, pie blanco
desc: De tamaño mediano. Sombrero de 5-10 (12) cm de diámetro, la cutícula se separa fácilmente, mate, seco, pardo rosado, rojo violáceo, crema, manchado de amarillo grisáceo, firme, sobre todo en la parte central. Láminas blancas, que amarillean de viejas, adnatas. Pie 3-8x 1,5-2 (3) cm, estrechado hacia la base, blanco. Carne blanca, firme, no amarga, de olor agradable. Rasgos característicos: sombrero firme, sobre todo la parte central; láminas blancas, normalmente débilmente manchadas de rosado, amarillentas de viejas. Crece aislada o en pequeños grupos. Una de las rúsulas más apreciadas. Común.

trumpakotis-minkstunis.habitat: Entre hierbas, lindes de bosque, bordes de caminos, parques, plazas, jardines
trumpakotis-minkstunis.season: Comienzo de la primavera, final del otoño
trumpakotis-minkstunis.features: Pie la mitad de largo que el diámetro del sombrero
desc: Carpóforos de tamaño mediano. Sombrero de 3-8 cm de diámetro, elástico, mate, fibroso, carnoso, gris parduzco negruzco sucio, color ceniza. Láminas jóvenes crema, viejas grises, adnatas. Pie 2—3x0,3—1,3 cm, del color del sombrero, engrosado en la parte inferior. Carne gruesa, blanda, pardo grisácea, con olor a madera, de sabor no amargo.
Rasgos característicos: carpóforos color ceniza sucio parduzco, carne no amarga.

Crece en pequeños grupos en bosques, parques, plazas, jardines, más en lugares abiertos. Comestible, común, sobre todo en los bordes herbosos de los caminos, en parques, incluso en plazas, junto a setos y vallas.

tusciakotis-baravykenis.features: Sombrero y pie de color castaño. Pie con un anillo grisáceo.
desc: Carpóforos de tamaño mediano. Sombrero de 6—10 cm de diámetro, a veces mayor, obtusamente cónico, aplanado, con mamelón, mate, seco, áspero - fibroso-escamoso, de color castaño, pardo rojizo. Tubos cortos (0,5-1 cm), amarillo verdosos, decurrentes por el pie. Poros grandes, dispuestos radialmente, laberínticos. Pie 4-5x 1-2 cm, que se engrosa ligeramente hacia la base, a veces se estrecha, con un pequeño anillo grisáceo, del color del sombrero. Carne amarillo pálido, correosa, sin olor ni sabor particulares, inmutable. Rasgos característicos: tubos cortos, poros laberínticos, grandes, carne inmutable.
